title: Every box lost money
lede: Pet food is heavy, bulky and cheap per pound. Customers could buy it at any supermarket. Shipping it to them one order at a time was the problem the company never solved.

blocks.title: What $100 of sales cost to deliver
blocks.subtitle: Costs per $100 of revenue: the prospectus description, the prospectus target, and reported quarterly actuals.
blocks.source: S-1 rows use the midpoints of stated ranges: product margins of 20–25% (product cost 75–80) and shipping costs of 100–110% of revenue, expected to fall to 20–25% once the Indianapolis center was at target volume[^1]. Actual rows are cost of goods sold and marketing & sales ÷ net sales from the 10-Qs[^2][^4]. In the filings, cost of goods sold includes outbound shipping. The dashed line marks $100, the break-even point.

blocks.title: Heavy, cheap, bulky
blocks.caption: Original drawing, not an official Pets.com asset.
blocks.body:
Litter and kibble are cheap to buy and expensive to ship. The prospectus put shipping at 100–110% of revenue in late 1999 and listed “shipping below our actual costs” as a risk.[^1] In the filings, cost of goods sold includes outbound shipping, and it ran above net sales in every quarter reported.[^2][^4]

We don’t repeat the widely told 40-lb-bag anecdotes: [we found no order-level data behind them](/about/#honesty).

blocks.title: What the gross margin counted
blocks.body:
Pets.com’s prospectus put fulfillment expenses in marketing and sales, not in cost of sales, which it defined as the cost of products plus outbound and inbound shipping.[^1] The Q3 2000 10-Q still lists distribution expenses and distribution payroll under marketing and sales.[^4] The gross margin that improved through 2000 therefore never carried the cost of picking and packing a box. Only the marketing view of the chart above does.

Pets.com did not disclose that cost in dollars. Its Petstore.com deal does show one rival’s. In a pro forma filing, Pets.com moved $2,959K of Petstore.com’s 1999 cost of goods sold, which was $5,161K as reported, into marketing and sales to match its own classification.[^48] Petstore.com’s net sales that year were 2,100,462 dollars, so the fulfillment cost alone was larger than its sales.[^48] For the first half of 2000 the move was $3,974K out of $10,163K, nearly as much as that half-year’s net sales.[^48]

Other delivery companies drew the line elsewhere. Kozmo booked delivery, mostly payroll for its delivery staff, as an operating expense below gross profit.[^50] PetSmart.com defined its cost of net revenues as products, promotional products and shipping.[^44] Headline gross margins from the four are not like-for-like, and we found no filing in which Pets.com changed its own classification.

The prospectus put shipping at **100–110% of revenue**[^1], before the cost of the food itself. Gross margin was **−64%** in Q1 2000 and **−20%** in Q2. It only reached **−3%** in Q3, “as our second distribution center in Indianapolis reached its full load.”[^4] When PETsMART.com took over the customers, its coupon excluded dog food, cat food and litter from the $25 minimum.[^36]

We found no primary source for the often-repeated story of a specific 40-lb bag sold at a set loss, so we don’t print one.
